title: Ki Tisa: the half shekel (Exodus 30:11–16)
hookLine: rich and poor give the same half coin; no one counts as whole alone

cards: A census sounds like the dullest thing in the world. But in the Torah, a head count carries a danger: the text warns of a plague coming with the counting.
So when Moses is told to count the Israelites, he's told not to count heads at all. Each one counted, from twenty years old and up, brings a coin, and the coins are counted instead. Here's the twist.
The coin isn't a whole one. It's half. And the richest family in the camp and the poorest hand over exactly the same thing.

teach.h: KI TISA: WHEN YOU LIFT THE HEAD.
teach.b: The portion is Ki Tisa, when you lift up, and the full phrase is when you lift up the head of the children of Israel: an old way of saying, when you take a count. To count someone is to lift their head.
Each one gives half a shekel, an offering to the Lord, and the text adds a line worth hearing slowly.

teach.h: NO MORE, NO LESS THAN HALF.
teach.b: In the JPS 1917 translation: "The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel." Plenty of gifts are measured by what you can afford. This one isn't.
Nobody can buy a bigger share of the count, and nobody is left out for lack of money.
The silver went to the service of the tent of meeting, and the text calls it a ransom for the soul, a covering, so that no plague would come with the counting.
Rashi passes on a midrash: Moses couldn't picture the coin, so God showed him a coin made of fire and said, like this. And why half? The Torah doesn't say.
One answer commentators give is simple: no one is complete alone.
You bring your half, someone else brings theirs, and only together does anything add up. Jews still remember the half shekel.
On a Shabbat just before the month of Adar, the passage is read aloud, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of the local money to charity.

how: The half-shekel passage is read as Parashat Shekalim on the Shabbat before Adar, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of their local currency to charity in its memory.

games.why: the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less. in this count, nobody can buy a bigger share.

practice: Think of something you're part of, a family, a team, a street, a congregation, and where it's waiting on your half: a dish washed, a message answered, ten minutes of help. Don't measure it against what anyone else gives.
Just picture everyone's halves adding up.
